Prepared for the office of the President, Supreme Court Bar Association, 2026–27

First we correct the record. Then we build recognition.

A three-week sprint that puts his own words back in front of the press, and a Hindi-first programme that makes him known for issues rather than for office, over the two years that follow.

Harsh Arya · Ninety-Eight · 15 October 2026 · Private and confidential Arrow keys, scroll or swipe to move · N for notes
Good afternoon. We are Ninety-Eight, a communications agency in Delhi NCR. This deck does two things. First it shows you what we found in the record, with a source on every slide, so you can check us. Then it proposes a way to work. We are proposing two jobs, not one: correcting the record on the October remarks, which is a three-week job, and building recognition among ordinary people, which is a two-year job that has to outlast a one-year term. We will take about twenty-five minutes, and we would rather be interrupted than finish uninterrupted. Nothing in here is a quote we have made up: every line attributed to the President, the Chief Justice or anyone else is on the record in the outlet named.
Why now

In four days of October his words reached two audiences, and each kept half.

10 OctThe detentionsFifty to sixty advocates detained near the Court; released after the CJI’s intervention.SupremeToday · The Swipe Up
12 OctThe mentionBefore the CJI: “We are not from any political party.”The Tribune · The News Minute
13 OctThe remarkTo the press: lawyers have a “legitimate constitutional right to express their views”.India Legal
Every source is listed in full in Appendix E.
Three days, three statements, and each was carried by English legal press, the national dailies and Hindi outlets, which is the reach of this office. On the tenth, fifty to sixty advocates were detained on Bhagwan Das Road as they tried to march to Jantar Mantar; the SCBA passed a resolution and wrote to the Chief Justice; the President posted on X that the detentions were “deeply disturbing” and demanded their release, then posted that the DCP had assured him they were being released. The Chief Justice later said, in court, that they were released on his verbal intervention. On the twelfth, mentioning the SCBA’s petition before the Chief Justice, the President said the Bar is not from any political party and that parties should not interfere in its domain. On the thirteenth he told the press that lawyers have a legitimate constitutional right to express their views even against the government, and that ideological differences should not undermine their shared duty to the Court. The pattern is that each outlet kept the half that suited it. That is the problem we are here about, and it is a narrower problem than it feels.

This is the record as it stands today, and we have kept to what is on it. Eighteenth of August: elected with 822 of 2,704 valid votes, more than eighty per cent of the 3,437 eligible advocates voting; the SCC Online result sheet lists eight candidates, Bar and Bench and LiveLaw list seven. He succeeded Vikas Singh and was Vice-President in 2021–22 and 2022–23. Nineteenth: in court the next morning, “Your Lordship is like a father figure. We will abide by your Lordship’s guidance. Your Lordship always guides us.” That is LiveLaw’s transcription, and the Hindi edition ran it too. Tenth of October: the detentions, the resolution, the X posts, the release. Eleventh: a Sunday special sitting of Justices Bagchi and Mohana on movement in the capital, and the Chief Justice declining a meeting with Mr Kharge and Mr Gandhi. Twelfth: the mention. The Tribune has him saying “We are not from any political party” and “Parties should not interfere in our domain”, and the Chief Justice saying “The Supreme Court should not be dragged into this.” The same day a small Hindi site quoted him, in the first person, saying Rahul Gandhi’s legal advisers do not know the law. We have not found that line in any larger outlet; whether he said it, and in what setting, is the first thing the fact base must settle, because it is exactly the kind of line that travels. Thirteenth: he told the press that lawyers have a legitimate constitutional right to express their views, even against the government, and that ideological differences should not undermine their shared duty to the Court; India Legal carried it the same day.

A third reading, from August, is deference: “CJI Like A Father Figure” ran in LiveLaw’s English and Hindi editions on 19 August.

The fix is consistency, not rebuttal: the same two-part sentence, every time, from him.
His actual position is institutional and two-sided. A: lawyers’ safety and their right to peaceful protest, which is the X post of the tenth, “Arbitrary detention and intimidation of advocates will not be tolerated,” and the remark to the press on the thirteenth. B: political parties must keep the Court out of their contests, which is the mention on the twelfth. Headlines flatten a two-part position to whichever half suits the outlet, and each side of the political divide hears only the half it dislikes. On the left, the half that reads as a line against the opposition: the Hindi site with the Rahul Gandhi line, and the national stories where his mention sits under the Chief Justice’s headline. On the right, the half that reads as a line against the police: the Hindi headline about the Cockroach Janta Party protest and the release, and India Legal on the intervention. Add the August “father figure” line and you have three readings of one man in eight weeks: deferential, anti-opposition, anti-police. None of them is what he said. The fix is not to argue with any one headline. It is to say the two-part sentence, in his words, once and clearly, and then to keep saying the same thing until the outlets copy it whole.

Two name variants are in use, “Pradeep Rai” and “Pradeep Kumar Rai”, and they return different first pages.
Three things are at stake, and the first is the Bar itself. He won roughly thirty per cent of the votes cast, in a divided house, and that house votes again in 2027. The Bar is his primary constituency and the office is theirs. Non-partisanship is the brand asset: anything that reads as a tilt toward government or opposition costs him the Bar first, and only then makes him a political target. The third thing is what a search shows today. We ran both name variants through our research tools on the fifteenth. Under “Pradeep Rai”, the election and the father-figure story lead. Under his full name, the first result is the May 2024 story about the plea to cancel his candidature, which the Court refused to entertain. We say indicative because it is not Google and not run from a Delhi device; the real audit, logged out, from Delhi, on both variants, is the first deliverable of the sprint. The point stands either way: two names, two first pages, and neither carries his own words.
Two jobs, not one

There are two jobs here, and they run on different clocks.

Phase 1Fix the recordweeks 0–3
Phase 2Positioningmonths 1–6

Guardrails, under all three
We do not use the controversy as the launch vehicle for awareness. That would weld it to his public identity. Each job opens its page.
We want to be precise about this because it decides the shape of the engagement. Correcting the record is a two-to-three-week job with a clear end: his words back in front of the press, factual errors corrected, one reference interview in each language on the first page of a search. Mass recognition is a twelve-to-twenty-four-month job, and it must outlast a one-year term, so it is built around issues and not around the office. The temptation is to use this month’s attention as the launch vehicle for the awareness work. We advise against it: it would weld the controversy to his public identity, and every later story would open with it. The three phases overlap but they do not merge. The guardrails sit under all three and we will come to them on their own slide, because for this audience they are the point.
Phase 1 · Fix the record · weeks 0 to 3

We put his own words back in front of the press once, with the context one click away.

Five deliverables, three weeks, and then you can stop.

Candidate outlets: Bar & Bench, LiveLaw, The Hindu or The Indian Express; Dainik Jagran, Amar Ujala, Hindustan or a Hindi TV legal segment. Appendix A.
Phase one is three weeks and five deliverables. The fact base first: the full video and a transcript of each remark, every headline in both languages, and a log that separates what an outlet got wrong from what it merely interpreted; only the first kind gets a rejoinder. Then one authoritative statement, issued once, in English and Hindi, with the full video attached, on his verified X account and the SCBA’s own channels, so that every journalist has the context one click away and nobody can say they could not find it. Then corrections, polite, to editors, for factual errors only. Then the reference interview: one long-form, on-record conversation with a credible legal-affairs journalist, Bar and Bench, LiveLaw, The Hindu or The Indian Express, and one Hindi equivalent, Dainik Jagran, Amar Ujala, Hindustan, or a Hindi television legal segment. Those two pieces become the thing a search returns for the next year. And spokesperson discipline: he speaks once, well; the Honorary Secretary or the Executive Committee speaks on internal Association matters, so that his voice is never the one attached to a disciplinary matter.

The office is already the megaphone: five outlets carry his statements the same day. Reach is not the constraint; consistency is. Every intervention maps to one pillar.

Search hygiene runs alongside: one name variant everywhere, identical bios, the knowledge panel claimed, no conflict-of-interest Wikipedia editing.
Phase two is positioning, and we are proposing three pillars rather than a persona. Each one is authentic to his record and legible to someone who has never been inside a courtroom. The safety and dignity of lawyers, which October already made his. The ordinary litigant: delays, cost and access, which is where his campaign stand against the sequencing system translates into something a litigant in Gorakhpur understands. And legal literacy, which we would name in Hindi, Jan-Nyay: what the Court said today, in plain language. His own story, a first-generation lawyer from Kushinagar who read at BHU and joined the profession in 1998, is the bridge to the district bars; it is told through the pillars, not as a pillar of its own. The office already carries his words into five outlets the same day, so reach is not the problem. Consistency is: every intervention he makes maps to one of the three, and anything that maps to none is not made. Search hygiene runs alongside: one name variant everywhere, identical bios, the knowledge panel claimed, and no editing of Wikipedia by anyone connected to him, because that is the one correction that becomes a story in itself.

Measured by Hindi video completion and shares, not follower counts. Most Indians do not know what the SCBA is; the issues are what they will know him for.
Phase three is the engine, and it is built on a reality check. Most Indians do not know what the SCBA is. The bar leaders the public recognises are known for causes and issues, not for the office they held. So recognition comes from issue association, delivered Hindi first, and sustained over time. Three parts. Hindi-first content: a short vertical explainer, “what the Supreme Court said today”, in sixty seconds and plain language, plus Hindi op-eds and Hindi television legal panels. A district-bar programme in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Delhi, because the lakhs of district-court advocates and their families are a mass constituency in their own right and an amplifier for everything else; he is one of them by biography. And long-form: podcasts and interviews on the pillars, never on the controversy. The strip underneath shows how one piece of work travels: a long-form interview once a quarter, cut into short clips for Hindi feeds, turned into weekly utility explainers that forward well on WhatsApp, and indexed so that a search in either name finds it. We measure completion and shares on Hindi video, not followers, because followers can be bought and completion cannot.
Guardrails

Four rules come before any of the above.

“An advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, either directly or indirectly.” Rule 36, Bar Council of India Rules, Part VI, Chapter II

No advertising, no solicitation

Issues and institutional work only; never his practice or clients. No influencer collaborations: the Bar Council has acted on online promotion since July 2024.

Nothing on pending matters

Including the SCBA’s own petition on the detentions, beyond the court record.

Two voices, kept apart

The Association’s voice and his own stay separate. Nothing goes out without his written sign-off.

No astroturfing

No fake accounts, bought followers, undisclosed paid posts or “independent” praise pieces. For an advocate the fallout is professional.

Every asset is checked for accuracy, dignity and compliance before it goes out. Sources: Madras HC, 3 July 2024, via Verdictum · BCI press release, 17 March 2025, via MediaNama.
For this room the guardrails are the proposal, so we give them a slide of their own. Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules: an advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, directly or indirectly. In July 2024 the Madras High Court directed the Bar Council to act against advocates advertising through online portals, and in March 2025 the Bar Council issued a press release condemning social-media promotion, influencer endorsements and celebrity promotions, with suspension or cancellation of enrolment as the sanction. So: no advertising and no solicitation; everything we make is about issues and institutional work, never his practice or his clients, and there are no influencer collaborations of any kind. Nothing on pending matters, including the Association’s own Article 32 petition on the detentions, beyond what is already on the record in court. The institutional voice and the personal voice are kept apart, and nothing goes out without his written sign-off. And no astroturfing: no fake accounts, no bought followers, no undisclosed paid posts, no “independent” praise pieces; for an advocate the fallout from that is professional. Our review checklist before anything goes out is three words: accuracy, dignity, compliance. If we ever come to you with a “growth hack”, you should end the engagement.

Four measures, and we take the baseline in week one before anything is published, so that the first monthly review compares against something. Search: a monthly audit of both name variants, and the test is whether his bio, the full statement and the reference interview are on page one. Media: monitoring split by language, with message pull-through, which asks a simple question of every story: did the outlet reproduce the two-part framing, or one half of it? Bar sentiment, tracked through his team and the Association’s channels, because that is the electorate. And social: completion and shares on Hindi video, not follower counts. A weekly dashboard, a monthly review in person, and a strategy reset each quarter, where we are as willing to stop something as to add it.

Appendix C shows the four formats so that nobody is imagining a billboard. The explainer: vertical, sixty seconds, Hindi with captions, one ruling in three sentences, and never a comment on a pending matter. The bilingual statement: two columns, English and Hindi, the full video linked, issued once. The Hindi op-ed: eight hundred words on one pillar, drafted for his review in his voice. And the district-bar hour: questions first, no speech, with one Hindi explainer recorded on the spot so that each visit leaves something behind. Every format is about issues and institutional work and never about his practice, which is what keeps it on the right side of Rule 36.

Appendix D exists because any search audit of his full name finds it, and your team should not be surprised by a journalist who has. On 15 May 2024 an advocate sought cancellation of his candidature for SCBA President, citing an FIR and other complaints. He told the Court there was no FIR, and the bench of Justices Surya Kant and K.V. Viswanathan refused to entertain the plea. That is the whole record as reported by Verdictum, and that is all we would ever say about it: if asked, the record in one sentence; never raised unprompted; and displaced in search by his own words over time, not suppressed. [For the room, not the slide: the petitioner was elected to the Association’s 2026–27 Executive Committee, per the SCC Online result sheet.]
